title: Aortic stenosis: managing it and replacing the valve

source.citation: Patel H, Lewis BW, Paulus R. Aortic Stenosis: Diagnosis and Treatment. Am Fam Physician. 2026;114(2):148-155.

questions.q: Which treatment slows or reverses aortic stenosis?
questions.a: None; management targets the comorbid conditions
questions.why: Optimising comorbidities reduces cardiovascular mortality even though it leaves the valve unchanged, so that is where the family physician's effort goes.

questions.q: Why is a statin still recommended for many patients with aortic stenosis?
questions.a: To reduce cardiovascular events by ten-year atherosclerotic risk, not to slow the stenosis
d: Because it reduces the need for valve replacement
Because it lowers the transaortic gradient
questions.why: The valve calcifies through an atherosclerosis-like pathway, which is why the statin trials were run. Atorvastatin 80 mg daily changed nothing on the valve.

questions.q: How should antihypertensive treatment be started in a patient with aortic stenosis?
questions.a: Start low and titrate slowly, to avoid vasodilation causing presyncope or syncope
d: Start at full dose to reach target quickly
questions.why: Uncontrolled blood pressure raises mortality in aortic stenosis, so the answer is to treat, just carefully. No single class has proven superior.

questions.q: In an asymptomatic patient, which echo surveillance intervals are correct?
questions.why: The interval shortens as severity rises because progression accelerates and symptoms often appear only once the valve is severely narrowed.

questions.q: Which clinical changes should trigger a repeat echo before the scheduled interval?
a: A newly absent second heart sound
questions.why: Each of these tracks the physiology: the murmur peaks later and the second heart sound fades as the valve stiffens.

questions.q: What activity advice fits moderate aortic stenosis?
questions.why: Mild stenosis gets no limits and severe stenosis is held to low intensity. Wearable data even suggest activity may be protective, though that is unproven.

questions.q: Which patients with aortic stenosis should be referred to cardiology?
questions.a: All with severe stenosis; consider referral for moderate
d: Only those with a bicuspid valve
questions.why: Referral is what gets the patient in front of a heart team of interventional cardiology, cardiothoracic surgery and anesthesia, which decides the timing of valve replacement.

questions.q: An asymptomatic patient has severe aortic stenosis. Which findings are indications for valve replacement?
questions.why: A rise in Vmax of more than 0.3 m/s within a year is the other trigger. Otherwise the patient stays under echo surveillance every 6 to 12 months.

questions.q: When is a supervised exercise stress test appropriate in aortic stenosis?
questions.a: In severe stenosis that appears asymptomatic, to unmask symptoms
d: In any symptomatic patient, to grade severity
In mild stenosis, to set the monitoring interval
Never, because of the risk of syncope
questions.why: A positive test is either symptoms of stenosis or a fall in systolic blood pressure of 10 mm Hg or more, and either one is an indication for replacement.

questions.q: How do transcatheter and surgical valve replacement compare on mortality?
questions.a: No difference in short- or long-term mortality, regardless of surgical risk
d: TAVR has lower mortality in high-risk patients only
TAVR has lower mortality at every risk level
questions.why: The two routes differ in complications rather than survival, and the choice turns on age, life expectancy and tolerance of anticoagulation.

questions.q: Which complications are more common after TAVR than after surgical valve replacement?
questions.why: Surgery carries the opposite pair: more new atrial fibrillation and more severe bleeding.

questions.q: A 58-year-old has symptomatic severe stenosis and a life expectancy of 25 years. Which approach is first-line?
questions.a: Surgical valve replacement, because long-term TAVR durability is unproven
d: TAVR, because it avoids open surgery
questions.why: The guideline's cutoffs are age 65 or younger, or a life expectancy over 20 years. Bicuspid valves do equally well by either route.

questions.q: A patient with a mechanical aortic valve also has atrial fibrillation. What is the INR goal?
questions.why: Without a risk factor the goal is 2.0 to 3.0. The other factors that raise it are prior venous thromboembolism, a known hypercoagulable state and left ventricular systolic dysfunction.

questions.q: After a surgical bioprosthetic aortic valve, what is the antithrombotic plan?
questions.a: A vitamin K antagonist for 3 to 6 months, then lifelong aspirin 75 to 100 mg
questions.why: After TAVR the first 3 to 6 months can be either a vitamin K antagonist or dual antiplatelet therapy, followed by the same lifelong aspirin.

questions.q: What is the preferred endocarditis prophylaxis before a dental procedure after aortic valve replacement?
questions.a: Amoxicillin 2 g as a single dose, 30 to 60 minutes before
d: Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days
Clindamycin 600 mg as a single dose
questions.why: The recommendation is expert consensus (SORT C) and applies to any prosthetic aortic valve, transcatheter or surgical.
